Decart's founders turned down a bigger offer from Nvidia to take Anthropic stock instead. Anthropic just walked away.

Bloomberg reported Monday that Anthropic completed due diligence on Israeli startup Decart and then abandoned a roughly $6B acquisition. It would have been the largest deal in Anthropic's history by an order of magnitude, weeks before its IPO.

What happened:

- Talks were first reported in August at about $6B, with the caveat that nothing was final
- Anthropic ran diligence, then withdrew
- Both companies declined to comment. The two sides may still collaborate, possibly as customer or investor
- Nobody has said whether Anthropic balked at the price or at something diligence surfaced

The detail that makes it painful, per Globes:

- Before the Anthropic talks, founders Dean Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev rejected an offer from Nvidia that was higher than Anthropic's
- They and their shareholders preferred Anthropic's offer in shares, in anticipation of the IPO
- They took paper in a company about to list at $2 trillion over more cash from the most valuable company on earth
- Then the buyer left. They now have neither

What Anthropic actually wanted, which most coverage got wrong:

- Decart is known publicly for world models and real-time video, including a virtual try-on product used by creators on Twitch, TikTok and YouTube
- The acquisition rationale was efficiency, not product. Decart's optimisation stack makes chips work harder across training and inference
- Its own site promises to squeeze every ounce of performance from every chip
- The logic was to let Anthropic's existing compute absorb more demand, while it commits hundreds of billions to capacity
- This was a deal about cost of goods sold, not a new product line

The numbers:

- Decart was valued at nearly $4B in May 2026, on a $300M round led by Radical Ventures
- That round included Nvidia, Adobe Ventures, Valor Equity Partners and Atreides, alongside Sequoia, Benchmark and Zeev Ventures
- Up from $3.1B in August 2025
- Total raised: about $450M
- The $6B price was roughly a 50% premium to the last private mark
- eBay is both an investor and a customer

Who is exposed:

- The May 2026 investors bought at $4B and would have been up about 1.5x in four months. They are now back to holding an unmarked private position
- Nvidia is on the cap table and also made the higher bid that got rejected. It is the one party here that can simply try again
- The founders and shareholders now have to find a new buyer, having already turned one down
- For Israel's AI sector this removes what would have been an Anthropic R&D presence in the country

The timing is the real story. Anthropic lists in weeks at a reported $2 trillion. A company heading into an IPO has two conflicting impulses: make the cost base look efficient, and make the acquisition history look disciplined. Buying Decart at a 50% premium would have helped the first and complicated the second. Diligence gave them a reason to choose discipline.

The entire game of building websites and apps could be about to change  and Runway might be leading the way.

Yesterday, Runway released something called Solaris, and it’s a seriously unusual system.

In simple terms: there’s no code, no Figma layout, and not even traditional HTML or CSS running in the browser. Instead, the AI generates live video frames in real time based on every click, drag, and interaction, effectively running the entire screen as an interactive video interface.

Think about how software usually works today.

A designer creates the interface, a developer writes the code, and then the browser renders that code into the final experience.

Solaris removes much of that middle layer.

The system works through a combination of two models. On the front end is Runway’s Gen-4.5 video engine, which generates the visual frames. Behind it is a language model that interprets what the user is trying to do.

Whenever you click a button or drag something across the screen, the language model instantly understands your intent and instructs the video model to generate the next frame accordingly.

And the result is happening live.

The demos Runway has released give you a glimpse of what this could mean.

Imagine a virtual showroom where you drag a shirt off a hanger and drop it onto your own photo — and the AI immediately generates a live try-on experience.

Or imagine a chemistry lesson where you mix an acid and a base, and instead of relying on traditional coded animations, the entire reaction appears interactively in front of you, generated on the fly.

That said, there’s an important caveat.

Solaris is nowhere near ready to replace traditional software in production environments.

With longer interactions, inconsistencies can appear between frames. Generating clean, readable text inside a video interface is still challenging. And the cloud-compute cost of generating every interaction and frame can be dramatically higher than running a conventional server-based application.

But the bigger idea is what really matters.

On one side, you have Google DeepMind’s Genie 3. On another, Anthropic’s increasingly capable models. And now Runway is exploring interfaces that are generated dynamically rather than rendered from traditional code.

The entire tech world seems to be moving toward a similar idea:

In the future, interfaces may not be something developers build line by line. They could be something AI generates dynamically through prompts, intent, and simulation.

At the end of the day, this may shift the value of software development away from simply knowing how to write code  and toward knowing how to imagine and design truly compelling user experiences.

So what do you think?

Will traditional software development eventually become mostly a backend concern, while AI handles the interfaces and experiences users actually interact with?

Drop your thoughts in the comments.

i genuinely did not expect a robot claw machine to make me think about ai differently but here we are.

been messing around with @axisrobotics for the past couple days. the pitch sounded off to me at first, control a virtual robot arm in your browser, no hardware, no download. 

felt like one of those crypto games where the “utility” is just an excuse to farm points. 

so i went in expecting nothing.

turns out every task you complete is a real recorded movement, timestamped, signed on chain, and actually used to train a robot to do that same thing in the real world. 

the reason it exists at all is kind of obvious once you sit with it. llms learned by reading the internet. 

robots don’t have an internet to learn from. nobody’s uploaded a million videos of “how to correctly grab a mug without dropping it” with the joint data attached. 

someone has to generate that from scratch, and apparently that someone can be me, on a laptop, at 1am.

what actually got me was the proof. 

their dataset didn’t just sit there, it pushed a real model from 83.9% to 88.8% success rate on an actual benchmark. 

that’s not marketing copy, that’s a published result. 

i’ve contributed real trajectories to that now and it’s a strange feeling knowing a robot somewhere might move a little better because of something i did on my laptop.

if you want to try it yourself, i’m using my link below, costs nothing but a few minutes and you get to see the whole thing live.

This paper tackles a huge blind spot in modern offline RL.

It asks an important question of why are we bloating actors with slow diffusion and flow-matching models when the critic is the one being discarded after training anyway?

In real-world robotics, taking multiple denoising steps per decision destroys control frequency.
 
They flip that tradeoff by shifting the architectural burden entirely to the training phase. 

Deepening MLP critics usually blows up in offline settings due to optimization collapse and bootstrap drift.

But they stabilize the critic using a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and categorical cross-entropy.

Because the deep critic does the heavy lifting, their framework (LAC) lets a bare-bones deterministic actor match the performance of heavy generative baselines on OGBench.

They also deliver up to 4x lower inference latency in a single forward pass & no distillation tricks are required.

So i feel its a super important read for everyone in RL.

Read the full paper here: https://t.co/ENSxOQII40

This paper is definitely one of the cleanest takes on offline RL we’ve come across recently.

We’ve all seen how messy the balance is between staying on-distribution and actually maximizing reward. 

Most people either throw in awkward penalties or just use diffusion models and live with painful sampling latencies.

They treat behavioral constraints and value optimization as motion fields in action space, blend them, and bake the whole thing into a one step generator. 

You get the expressiveness of a generative model without having to wait on multi step denoising at test time, just a single forward pass.

They tested it on 73 tasks across D4RL and OGBench and took the top average rank against some serious diffusion and flow baselines. 

Definitely worth reading if you care about fast continuous control: https://t.co/FWtPTmNFiK
